posts.title: My Chemical Romance at Hollywood Bowl: which 2026 night?
posts.seoTitle: MCR Hollywood Bowl: which night? | TourTicketCompare
posts.description: Compare My Chemical Romance's October 2026 Hollywood Bowl dates, guest billing and start times before choosing a night and checking ticket totals.
posts.summary: My Chemical Romance's five October Hollywood Bowl listings are not identical. The first three carry The Black Parade 2026 billing; the final two name different special guests and start an hour earlier.
posts.author: TourTicketCompare

sections.content:
Choose the billing you want before comparing tickets. My Chemical Romance's Hollywood Bowl dates on 21, 23 and 24 October carry **The Black Parade 2026** title. The 30 October listing names **The Used** as special guest; 31 October names **Thrice**. Those final two listings also start an hour earlier. The same artist and venue do not make these five purchases interchangeable.

The [My Chemical Romance date board](/artists/my-chemical-romance) is the starting point for comparing ticket options for the exact night you choose. A figure on a different night's card is not a quote for your preferred show.

sections.title: The five nights, side by side
sections.content:
These are the event titles and scheduled start times in TTC's verified records, inspected on 11 October 2026. The promoter's listings and the label's announcement support the dates and billing below. Times are local to Los Angeles; they are scheduled event starts, not confirmed doors or stage times. Recheck the current event listing before booking.

| Date in October 2026 | Event billing | Scheduled start |
|---|---|---|
| Wednesday 21 | My Chemical Romance The Black Parade 2026 | 8pm |
| Friday 23 | My Chemical Romance The Black Parade 2026 | 8pm |
| Saturday 24 | My Chemical Romance The Black Parade 2026 | 8pm |
| Friday 30 | My Chemical Romance with Special Guest The Used | 7pm |
| Saturday 31 | My Chemical Romance with Special Guest Thrice | 7pm |

The [Warner Records announcement](https://press.warnerrecords.com/sites/g/files/g2000014901/files/2025-09/MY%20CHEMICAL%20ROMANCE%20ANNOUNCE%20%20THE%20BLACK%20PARADE%202026.pdf) identifies the first three as the tour's closing North American run. Live Nation separately lists [30 October with The Used](https://www.livenation.com/event/vvG1iZbS55yKJr/my-chemical-romance-with-special-guest-the-used) and [31 October with Thrice](https://www.livenation.com/event/vvG1iZbS55BdJV/my-chemical-romance-with-special-guest-thrice).

sections.title: What the different billing lets you decide
sections.content:
If seeing The Used is part of the reason for going, shortlist 30 October. If it is Thrice, shortlist 31 October. If the advertised Black Parade tour is the attraction, start with 21, 23 and 24 October and read the specific event details before paying.

That is a useful distinction, but it has a boundary: **an event title is not a setlist**. The later listings do not establish which MCR songs will be played, and the Halloween date alone does not establish a special performance. Nothing in this comparison promises a particular song or an identical show across nights. Guest billing can change; recheck the promoter's event page when booking.

There is a practical difference even if the guest does not matter to you. A 7pm start leaves an hour less for getting from work or a flight to the venue than an 8pm start. Check the event's arrival instructions separately. Do not treat either scheduled start as the time MCR will take the stage.

sections.title: Compare tickets within your shortlist
sections.content:
Once the night is fixed, compare the same quantity and the same kind of seat. A pair together, two separate seats and a single ticket answer different needs, even when their first displayed figures look similar. Check section, row, seat arrangement and any view restriction on the provider's listing. The [ticket-listing guide](/guides/how-to-read-a-ticket-listing) explains those fields.

The [MCR ticket-price page](/artists/my-chemical-romance/ticket-prices) organises tracked dates and any eligible provider-listed snapshots by city. Use each date's own comparison links. Any displayed figure belongs to that event and provider at the capture time shown; it is not a final checkout total or evidence that a particular seat remains purchasable.

If several nights suit you, open each separately and compare actual listings that meet your needs, including the final order total. There is no supported claim here that a Wednesday, a Halloween show or a later-added date costs less. The [comparison guide](/guides/how-to-compare-concert-ticket-prices) covers how to check totals without mixing unlike tickets.

sections.title: Keep the date attached to the purchase
sections.content:
Before paying, match the full date on the listing and order summary to the night you selected. Then check the ticket delivery deadline against your travel plans. A confirmation email and a transferred ticket are different things; the [delivery and transfer guide](/guides/ticket-delivery-and-transfer-timing) explains what to confirm with a resale seller.

The useful order is simple: billing, date, seats, total, delivery. Comparing figures first can leave you with a ticket for a concert you did not mean to choose.

Live Nation — October 31 listing with Thrice
Warner Records — The Black Parade 2026 tour announcement

posts.title: Trans-Siberian Orchestra 2026: matinee or evening tickets?
posts.description: Choosing Trans-Siberian Orchestra tickets for 2026? Check afternoon and evening sessions, family logistics and the exact start time before comparing.
posts.summary: Several stops on Trans-Siberian Orchestra's 2026 winter tour have two performances on the same day. Choose the session your group can attend, then compare tickets for that exact performance.
posts.author: TourTicketCompare

sections.content:
Choose a Trans-Siberian Orchestra matinee if an earlier start fits your group and journey home; choose the evening if the afternoon clashes with work or travel. **Neither session is established as the less expensive option by the evidence here.** For the 2026 winter tour, several cities have two performances on the same date, so the start time is part of identifying the ticket you need.

Start with the [Trans-Siberian Orchestra date board](/artists/trans-siberian-orchestra), then check the full date and time on the provider's listing. Matching the city and day is not enough when the venue hosts both sessions.

sections.title: Confirmed examples of two-show days
sections.content:
The following schedules were checked against official artist or venue pages on 11 October 2026. All times are local to the venue. This is a selection of confirmed examples, not the complete tour schedule.

| Date in 2026 | City and venue | Afternoon | Evening |
|---|---|---|---|
| Saturday 21 November | Denver — Ball Arena | 3pm | 7.30pm |
| Saturday 5 December | Columbus — Nationwide Arena | 3pm | 7.30pm |
| Sunday 20 December | Philadelphia — Xfinity Mobile Arena | 3pm | 7.30pm |

TSO's [Denver page](https://www.trans-siberian.com/pages/market/denver--co?event=Denver_CO) and [Philadelphia page](https://www.trans-siberian.com/pages/market/philadelphia--pa?event=Philadelphia_PA) list both sessions. [Nationwide Arena's Columbus listing](https://www.nationwidearena.com/events/detail/trans-siberian-orchestra-6) does the same.

TTC currently tracks the afternoon performance in each of these three examples. An evening session missing from the date board does not mean the performance does not exist. Use the official schedule to confirm the session you want; the site's checked comparison links apply only to the performance named on their card.

sections.title: An afternoon ticket is still a ticket to the advertised production
sections.content:
The official pages describe the 2026 tour as a new staging of **The Ghosts of Christmas Eve**, followed by a second set. They do not label the afternoon performances as shortened children's shows. Equally, that description does not promise identical running times or song selections across sessions.

For a family booking, an earlier start may make the journey home easier to plan. It does not make the production quieter: the event descriptions mention lasers, pyrotechnics and other effects. Check the venue's child admission, hearing protection and accessibility guidance before choosing seats. Do not assume a child enters free or can share an adult's seat.

For an evening booking, work backwards from the scheduled start to the time you need to arrive. A 7.30pm listing is not a confirmed finishing time. If the last train or bus determines whether the evening works, ask the venue about expected timings before committing.

sections.title: Compare one performance at a time
sections.content:
The easy mistake is opening two listings for the same date and assuming they describe the same event. Check **city, venue, date and start time** before comparing section, row and ticket quantity. A 3pm ticket should not be treated as admission to the 7.30pm performance unless the actual ticket terms explicitly say so.

For sessions TTC tracks, the [TSO ticket-price page](/artists/trans-siberian-orchestra/ticket-prices) brings together the date-specific comparison links and any eligible listed-price snapshots. A displayed figure is one provider's snapshot for that performance, with its capture time. It does not describe the evening session, a family bundle or the final order total.

A group needs a listing that meets its seating requirements, rather than a headline figure for a single seat. Confirm whether the seats are together and compare the total for everyone attending. The [listing guide](/guides/how-to-read-a-ticket-listing) and [ticket-price comparison guide](/guides/how-to-compare-concert-ticket-prices) cover those checks.

sections.title: Delivery matters when someone else is taking the group
sections.content:
If you are buying as a gift or for relatives, establish who will hold the tickets on show day. Nationwide Arena says its mobile tickets are not valid as paper printouts or screenshots; its event page explains the arrangements for guests without a smartphone. Those are Columbus instructions, not a rule to assume for every tour stop.

Check the chosen venue's own entry method and the seller's delivery deadline. The [delivery and transfer guide](/guides/ticket-delivery-and-transfer-timing) helps distinguish an order confirmation from a ticket ready for entry. Choosing the right session is only useful if the person going can receive and use the tickets.

posts.title: Bruno Mars at Falcon Stadium: September 2026 entry guidance
posts.seoTitle: Bruno Mars: Falcon Stadium entry 2026 | TourTicketCompare
posts.description: Entry guidance for Bruno Mars’ 26–27 September 2026 Falcon Stadium concerts. These dates have passed; find current dates on the artist page.
posts.summary: The 26–27 September 2026 Falcon Stadium dates have passed. This article records the access guidance for those concerts, not the arrangements for a future event. For upcoming shows, start with the current Bruno Mars date list and check the instructions for that exact show.
posts.author: TourTicketCompare

sections.content:
**These concert dates have passed.** The guidance below relates to the 26 and 27 September 2026 Falcon Stadium dates listed on Bruno Mars’ official tour page. It should not be used as the access plan for a future concert. [Check current Bruno Mars dates and ticket links](/artists/bruno-mars) for upcoming shows, then read the venue's instructions for the date you choose.

Falcon Stadium is inside the United States Air Force Academy, so the September 2026 guidance covered access to the installation as well as the stadium. A concert ticket identifies the show and admission category; access instructions need to be checked separately for everyone travelling together.

sections.title: Start with the instructions for your concert
sections.content:
The Academy’s general visitor page describes sponsored passes, identification checks and screening. It also recognises special-event access arrangements. Those general rules are useful background, but they are not enough to tell every concertgoer which pass, gate or registration process applies on their date.

Read the Academy’s concert information and the messages attached to your booking before you travel. If they do not explain your circumstances, ask the Academy’s Pass and Registration Office to confirm. Do not use a registration link for a different event, or assume that an ordinary visitor pass covers your concert.

Check for each person in your group whether advance registration is required, which original identification they need, and whether their citizenship or documents require an in-person visit. The Academy publishes separate instructions for non-U.S. citizens. Its published office hours have not always agreed between one section of the site and another, so confirm any appointment you need directly with the office rather than planning around a quoted opening time.

sections.title: Match the arrival plan to your ticket
sections.content:
The Academy’s floor-seating guidance directs floor ticketholders through the South Gate and into the stadium at Gate 3, with wristband collection inside. It also gives separate instructions for rideshare arrivals. Read that guidance if you hold a floor ticket; do not assume the same route applies to every seating category.

Before leaving, keep the concert date, ticket category, parking or rideshare instructions and entry guidance together. If friends bought different ticket types, compare the instructions before agreeing a meeting point. Leave time for the checks described by the Academy and consult the latest event guidance for arrival times.

The concert has its own published bag policy too. Check its size limits and exceptions before packing, particularly if you need to carry medical items or supplies for an infant. A bag accepted at another venue may not meet this event’s rules.

sections.title: What the ticket comparison can tell you
sections.content:
The [Bruno Mars page](/artists/bruno-mars) lists the verified dates with provider links checked for each event. Any price shown is one ticket site’s listed price, with when it was checked. It doesn’t include a promise about installation access, a particular seat or your final checkout total.

Open the button for your chosen date and check the provider’s event, seating and delivery details. Keep that ticket check separate from the Academy’s access instructions: completing one does not establish that the other is complete. The [delivery and transfer guide](/guides/ticket-delivery-and-transfer-timing) explains what to check when tickets will reach your account later.

posts.title: Buying tickets for a concert in another country
posts.seoTitle: Concert tickets abroad: what to check | TourTicketCompare
posts.description: Following a tour to another country adds time zones, currency, local ticket sites and different resale rules. What to check before buying and booking travel.
posts.summary: Major tours now cross continents, and plenty of fans follow them. Buying for a show abroad adds a handful of checks that a home-town ticket never needs, from the time zone of the sale to the currency of the total and the rules that apply to resale where the show takes place.
posts.author: TourTicketCompare

sections.content: Plenty of the biggest tours on TourTicketCompare cross borders. [Harry Styles](/artists/harry-styles) has dates listed in the United States, Canada, Australia, Ireland, Spain and the UK; [Karol G](/artists/karol-g) in the United States and across Europe; [Oasis](/artists/oasis) in Scotland, England, Ireland, Germany, Spain and the Netherlands; and [BTS](/artists/bts) in Australia. For some fans the nearest date, or the only one left, is in another country. Buying a ticket for that show works much like buying one at home, with a handful of extra checks that are easy to miss.

sections.title: Read every time in the right zone
sections.content:
Two different clocks matter: the on-sale time and the show time. An on-sale announced for 10am usually means 10am where the venue is, not where you are. Convert it before the day, and check whether either country changes its clocks between now and then. The [onsale preparation guide](/guides/how-to-prepare-for-a-ticket-onsale) covers the rest of the routine.

The show date needs the same care once travel is involved. A late show that ends after midnight can matter for the last train, the hotel booking and the flight home.

sections.title: Know which ticket site covers that country
sections.content:
Large ticket sites often run separate country sites, and an account on one does not always carry over to another. Before the sale, find out which site the venue or tour names for that country, create the account in advance if you need one, and confirm that it accepts your card and billing address. Mobile tickets can also depend on the ticket site's app for that region, so check that you can install and sign in to it.

If the ticket is transfer-locked or tied to a name, make sure the name on the order matches the identification you will carry. Some venues ask to see it at the gate.

sections.title: Compare totals in one currency
sections.content:
A total in euros, pounds or Australian dollars is not comparable with one in US dollars until both are converted (the [currency converter](/currency-converter) does this with reference rates), and your card may add its own conversion charge on top. Compare final checkout totals for the same number of tickets, then work out what your card will actually charge. The [fees guide](/guides/concert-ticket-fees-explained) lists the charges that tend to appear late.

Fee rules differ by country as well. In the United States, the FTC's rule on unfair or deceptive fees requires mandatory fees to be included in the upfront price of live-event tickets, although taxes, shipping and optional add-ons can still be shown separately. Other countries set their own rules, so read the order summary rather than assuming the first price shown is the one you pay.

sections.title: Resale rules follow the venue, not you
sections.content: Resale rules are set where the event takes place. In the UK, for example, section 90 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 requires a ticket resold through a secondary ticketing platform to come with the information needed to identify the seat or standing area, any restriction on who may use it, and its face value. That protection applies to UK events wherever the buyer lives. Other countries restrict resale differently, and some tours add their own terms, so read the terms attached to the specific ticket before buying it second-hand.

sections.title: Book travel you can change
sections.content: Tickets can arrive late, and shows can be rescheduled. Until the ticket is in your account and the date is settled, flexible or refundable travel is worth more than it would be for a local show. If a date moves, the [postponement and cancellation guide](/guides/what-to-do-if-a-concert-is-postponed-or-cancelled) explains what to check first.

sections.title: Using the artist pages from abroad
sections.content: Each artist page lists dates with a checked ticket link for that exact show, with the city and country shown on each date. Where a price appears, it is one provider's listed price in the currency that provider listed, with the time it was checked. Open the provider's page to confirm the currency, the fees and the final total before buying.

sources.label: UK Consumer Rights Act 2015, section 90 — information for resold tickets
US Federal Trade Commission — Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees, FAQs

posts.title: Choosing a Harry Styles night at Madison Square Garden
posts.seoTitle: Choosing a Harry Styles MSG night | TourTicketCompare
posts.description: Harry Styles’ 2026 MSG residency repeats the same venue across 30 nights. Check the exact date, ticket details and delivery terms before buying.
posts.summary: A residency breaks the habit most ticket buyers rely on. When the artist, the tour and the venue are identical across every listing, the date is the only thing distinguishing what you are about to buy — and it is the field people skim.
posts.author: TourTicketCompare

sections.content:
Most ticket buying leans on a shortcut nobody articulates: you recognise the city, you recognise the venue, and you assume that between them they have identified the show. A residency quietly removes that shortcut. Madison Square Garden announced Harry Styles' Together, Together run as 30 consecutive shows at the arena, every Wednesday, Friday and Saturday from 26 August to 31 October 2026. Every listing therefore carries the same artist, the same tour name and the same building. The date is doing all the work of telling one from another, and the date is the field people skim.

As of 5 October 2026, the run is past its halfway point. Twelve nights remain on that schedule, from Wednesday 7 October to Saturday 31 October. A listing for a night that has already happened is worthless, and with eighteen past nights in the same building, it is an easy mistake to make.

sections.title: The venue name is not an identifier here
sections.content:
For a single-night stop, the artist and venue may be enough to identify the show. For this residency, they are not. A resale listing, a screenshot sent by a friend, a search result, an old browser tab — none of them are self-identifying, and two of them can look identical while pointing at nights weeks apart.

The practical version of this is short. Take the date from the card on the [Harry Styles page](/artists/harry-styles), open the ticket site through that date's own button, then check the date twice more: once on the provider's listing, once on the order summary before you pay. The order summary is the one that counts, because it is the last screen where a mistake is still free to fix.

A distinctive listing title is still not a substitute for the event date. Check the full calendar date on the listing and order summary, even when the artist and building look familiar.

sections.title: What genuinely differs between the nights
sections.content:
Less than people assume, which is worth saying plainly rather than manufacturing distinctions.

Ticketmaster's tour announcement says Jamie xx opens all Madison Square Garden dates, so the support billing is not a reason to pick one night over another. Doors, stage times and the venue's own entry rules are Madison Square Garden's to set and publish, and they are published per event rather than per residency — the venue's FAQs are the place to read them, not a third-party page.

The original sale schedule was staggered, but not by months. Ticketmaster lists general sale for the first twenty shows on 30 January 2026, split between two times, and for the final ten on 4 February. Those dates explain the original release structure; they do not establish today’s prices or availability. Compare the listings for the nights you can attend, including the ticket category, seat details, fees and delivery terms.

sections.title: Where the artist page can and cannot help
sections.content:
The date board on the artist page carries the nights verified from the source, each with the ticket sites that have their own checked destination for that exact night. Where a figure appears next to a button, it is one provider's listed price for that one night, captured at the time shown beside it — per-date, never per-residency. That is the whole reason the site does not publish a "prices for the Harry Styles residency" number: there is no such thing, only 30 separate sets of listings that happen to share an address.

Two limits are worth stating. First, a night that is not on the artist page is a night that has not been verified, which is not the same as a night that does not exist — the venue's own announcement is the authority on the shape of the run. Second, nothing on the artist page describes a seat. Section, row, obstruction notes and delivery method live on the provider's listing, and for a building with as many seat categories as this one, the [guide to reading a ticket listing](/guides/how-to-read-a-ticket-listing) is more useful than any figure.

If you take one thing from this: on a residency, treat the date as the identifier and everything else as decoration.

posts.title: Floor or seats at a stadium concert: how to choose
posts.seoTitle: Stadium concert: floor or seats? | TourTicketCompare
posts.description: A floor ticket and a seat at the same stadium show are different products. How to choose between them, and what to check on a listing before paying.
posts.summary: At a stadium show, the choice between the floor and a seat decides more than the view. It sets when you need to arrive, how long you stand, what an early-entry add-on is worth and how to read a resale listing. Here is how to weigh it before you compare prices.
posts.author: TourTicketCompare

sections.content: Most price comparisons for a stadium concert quietly assume the tickets being compared are the same kind of thing. They often are not. A floor ticket and a seat in the bowl on the same night are different products with different costs attached, and several of those costs never appear in the price. Deciding which one you want first makes every later comparison fairer.

sections.title: Three things "floor" can mean
sections.content:
The word covers more than one arrangement, and the listing should tell you which.

- **General admission standing.** You have a place on the floor, not a spot. Where you end up depends on when you arrive and how crowded the area is.
- **Reserved floor seats.** Chairs are set out on the pitch or floor, each with a section, row and seat number, just like the bowl.
- **Early-entry or package floor tickets.** A general admission ticket sold with earlier access. Ticketmaster's help page for The Unraveled Tour, for example, describes its GA Early Entry Experience as a general admission ticket with priority access to the floor, alongside early entry into the venue.

If a listing just says "floor" without a section, a row or the words "general admission", ask which it is before paying. The [guide to reading a ticket listing](/guides/how-to-read-a-ticket-listing) covers the other labels worth checking.

sections.title: What the floor costs besides money
sections.content:
A general admission floor ticket is paid for partly in time. A spot near the stage usually means arriving early and standing for the support act as well as the headliner. Packages that sell early entry exist precisely because floor position is decided by arrival order, which tells you how much the queue matters.

The floor can also come with its own entry process. At Falcon Stadium, the Air Force Academy's floor-seating guidance for the September 2026 Bruno Mars shows sent floor ticketholders through a specific gate, with wristbands collected inside. That is typical of stadium shows: the floor is often managed separately from the bowl, so read the venue's instructions for your ticket type rather than a friend's.

Accessibility is a separate question again. If you need step-free access, somewhere to sit, or space for a companion, check the venue's accessible seating arrangements directly; a standing floor ticket may not meet those needs.

sections.title: What a seat buys you
sections.content: A seat in the lower bowl or stands gives you a fixed place, a view that does not depend on the people in front of you, and freedom to arrive later. On a large stage the height can be an advantage, because you see the whole production and the screens instead of the backs of heads. The trade is distance from the stage, and on some layouts side-stage or partial-view seats that are priced lower for a reason. Listings that say "limited view" or "side stage" deserve a look at the venue's seating map before you decide.

sections.title: Compare like with like
sections.content:
Once you know which product you want, compare only that product. A general admission floor listing is not a cheaper version of a reserved floor seat, and a side-stage seat is not a cheaper version of a centre one. Match the admission type, the section and the number of tickets, then compare final checkout totals rather than first displayed prices. The [price comparison guide](/guides/how-to-compare-concert-ticket-prices) walks through that step by step.

Delivery matters more on the floor than it seems. Wristband and early-entry arrangements can depend on the ticket being in the right account on the day, so check when a resale ticket will actually arrive; the [delivery and transfer guide](/guides/ticket-delivery-and-transfer-timing) explains the usual gaps.

sections.title: Where to start
sections.content: Stadium runs listed on TourTicketCompare include [Oasis](/artists/oasis) at Celtic Park, the Etihad Stadium and Knebworth, [Metallica](/artists/metallica) across North American stadiums, [Bruno Mars](/artists/bruno-mars) and [Harry Styles](/artists/harry-styles). Each artist page lists dates with a checked ticket link for that exact show. Where a price appears, it is one provider's listed price at the time shown, for whatever ticket that provider listed, so open the provider's page to confirm whether it is a floor or seated ticket before comparing.

posts.title: Oasis Live '27: what a code-only ticket sale changes
posts.seoTitle: Oasis Live '27 tickets: the code sale | TourTicketCompare
posts.description: Oasis Live '27 tickets go only to registered fans with a unique code. What that means for codes offered online, resale listings and choosing a night.
posts.summary: Oasis Live '27 was sold only to registered fans with codes, and the band announced on 27 September 2026 that every Oasis Live '27 ticket has been sold. Official resale opens nearer the shows, at the original price, through Ticketmaster and Twickets only. That changes how to read almost every ticket offer you will see for these dates.
posts.author: TourTicketCompare

sections.content:
**Update, 5 October 2026:** on 27 September 2026 the official Oasis site announced that every Oasis Live '27 ticket has been sold. It says resale tickets will not be available until nearer the events, and then only at the price originally paid, through Ticketmaster and Twickets. Any ticket offered for these dates anywhere else, or before that resale opens, is outside the official process. Wait for those official channels rather than buying it.

The official Oasis site said registration for Oasis Live '27 tickets had closed, and that selected registrants would receive a unique code, with full details of how to buy, by email between 24 and 27 September 2026. Consequence reported that each code is non-transferable and tied to an assigned on-sale window, that sales would begin on Friday 25 September at times varying by city, and that there would be no general on-sale or other public pre-sale. Those few sentences change how nearly every ticket offer for these dates should be read.

sections.title: If you registered: trust the email, not the feed
sections.content:
The code and the buying instructions came by email from the official process. If you still hold an unused code, read that email for three things: the city and date it covers, the start time of its window, and the time zone that start time is written in. The tour runs from Glasgow to Manchester, mainland Europe, the United States, Slane and Knebworth, so an on-sale time quoted without a zone can easily be an hour, or many hours, away from your own.

Because reports describe the codes as non-transferable, anyone offering to sell or "share" an Oasis code is offering something the process says cannot be passed on. Treat that as a warning sign, not a shortcut. The same goes for messages asking you to "confirm" a code through a link that did not come from the official email. The [guide to avoiding ticket scams](/guides/how-to-avoid-ticket-scams) covers the payment and contact patterns worth refusing outright.

sections.title: If you did not get a code
sections.content:
With no general sale, a fan without a code has no second official queue to join. The official route left is resale, and the Oasis site says that opens nearer the events, at the price originally paid, through Ticketmaster and Twickets only. Until then, any ticket you are offered sits outside that process, whatever the listing calls it.

Two checks carry most of the weight. First, the channel and timing: an offer on any other site, or before official resale opens, deserves a direct question about what is actually being sold and whether it will ever be delivered. Second, terms: the organiser's own ticket terms decide whether a resold ticket will scan, so read them before paying for one. The [official versus resale guide](/guides/primary-vs-resale-concert-tickets) sets out the general differences.

For the UK dates there is a helpful legal floor. Section 90 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 requires that a ticket resold through a secondary ticketing platform for a UK event comes with the information needed to identify the seat or standing area, any restriction on who may use the ticket, and the face value, meaning the price stated on the ticket. NBC News reported that promoters said standard ticket prices for this tour are fixed. Together with the face-value-only official resale, those mean a UK listing asking more than the ticket originally cost is not part of the official process.

sections.title: Pick the night before the price
sections.content:
Several venues on this tour host long runs: eleven nights at the Etihad Stadium in Manchester, five at Celtic Park in Glasgow, and a series at Knebworth. When the artist, the tour and the stadium are identical across listings, the date is the only field separating one ticket from another, and it is the one people skim. Confirm the date on the listing, then again at checkout, then on the ticket itself once it reaches your account.

Standing and seated tickets at the same stadium are different products too, even on the same night. The [guide to reading a ticket listing](/guides/how-to-read-a-ticket-listing) explains how to confirm section, row and admission type before comparing prices.

sections.title: What the Oasis page shows
sections.content: The [Oasis page](/artists/oasis) lists the dates that have a checked ticket link for that exact show, so a date appears there once its link has been verified rather than when it is announced. Where a price appears, it is one provider's listed price at the time shown next to it. It is not the tour's face value, it is not a code-holder's price, and it is not a final checkout total. TourTicketCompare does not issue codes, run the registration or sell tickets.

NBC News reported that promoters said standard ticket prices for the tour are fixed. Put those two facts together and the picture is simple: the official price is set once, for the fans holding codes, and any price you see moving is a resale price.

sections.title: Compare prices for the date you want
sections.content:
[See Oasis resale ticket prices by date](/artists/oasis/ticket-prices) for the lowest listed price on each night, the ticket site listing it and when it was checked. [Choose your city and concert night on the Oasis date board](/artists/oasis), then open the checked ticket links for that exact show. Where a card shows current listed prices, use them to decide which listings to inspect first. Keep the date, ticket quantity and seated or standing area fixed when comparing providers; a lower starting price for a different night or ticket type is a different purchase. Confirm the final total and current availability on the provider before paying.

sections.title: A price here is a resale price, not what the ticket cost
sections.content:
Where an Oasis date on this site carries a figure, it comes from a resale provider: Vivid Seats, TicketNetwork or StubHub International, each only for a listing checked against that exact date. The figure is that one provider's listed price at the time printed beside it. It is not the face value, it is not what a code-holder paid, and it does not establish the final total for the tickets you select.

Do not assume mandatory fees will always be added later. In the US, the FTC's live-event ticket fee rule requires mandatory fees in the upfront total; government charges, shipping and optional add-ons may be shown separately before payment. Other countries have their own rules. Check what the actual listing includes, then compare the final amount for your quantity, currency and selected extras. The [guide to ticket fees](/guides/concert-ticket-fees-explained) provides the checkout checklist.

A date with no figure is not a date with no tickets. It means no provider had a checked, current figure for it when the page was built. StubHub International links open stubhub.ie, whichever country the show is in, and the [StubHub International guide](/guides/stubhub-international-explained) explains why.

This post deliberately gives no face-value price list. The official sale is where those prices are set, and a number copied from elsewhere would be one more figure to check rather than one you can rely on.

sections.title: Every night is its own market
sections.content:
The tour stays put for long runs: eleven nights at the Etihad Stadium in Manchester, five at Celtic Park in Glasgow, six at Knebworth. The artist, tour and stadium are identical across each run, but resale prices are not. Each night has its own sellers and its own buyers, so a figure for one night tells you nothing about the next.

That is why the [Oasis page](/artists/oasis) prices each date on its own card, and why priced cards have a "Show price history" button. The history lists earlier prices checked for that date, so you can see whether today's figure is typical of what that night has shown or out of line with it. It is still a record of listed prices from one provider at a time, not a forecast. The [guide to how resale pricing works](/guides/how-resale-ticket-pricing-works) covers why asking prices move the way they do.

sections.title: The rules that let you check a listing
sections.content:
For the Glasgow, Manchester and Knebworth dates, section 90 of the UK Consumer Rights Act 2015 applies to a ticket resold through a secondary ticketing platform. The buyer must be given the ticket's face value, the information needed to identify the seat or standing area, and any restriction on who may use the ticket. So on a UK listing, the face value should be on the page. Compare it with the asking price before you decide whether the gap is one you accept.

Ireland goes further. Its Sale of Tickets Act 2021 prohibits selling a ticket above its original sale price for designated events and events at designated venues. Whether a particular show is covered depends on that designation, so for the Slane Castle dates, check the listing and the organiser's terms rather than assuming either way.

The mainland European dates in Munich, Barcelona and Amsterdam, and the US dates in Foxborough and Las Vegas, fall under their own local rules, which this post does not cover. Everywhere, the organiser's ticket terms decide whether a resold ticket will get you in. The [official versus resale guide](/guides/primary-vs-resale-concert-tickets) sets out what to check before paying.

sections.title: What to take from a figure
sections.content: Use a figure to narrow down which night and which provider to look at, then open the listing itself. Confirm the date, the standing or seated area and, on UK dates, the face value, then read the total on the provider's order summary. That total is the number to judge, not the figure that brought you there.

posts.title: Three kinds of Olivia Rodrigo ticket, and what each one means
posts.seoTitle: Unraveled Tour ticket types explained | TourTicketCompare
posts.description: Standard, VIP and Silver Star tickets are sold differently on The Unraveled Tour, and the differences follow the ticket onto the resale market.
posts.summary: An Unraveled Tour ticket is not one product. The tour sells standard tickets, VIP packages and a request-based fixed-price ticket, and the rules attached to each — transferability, delivery timing, identity checks — decide what a second-hand listing is actually worth buying.
posts.author: TourTicketCompare

sections.content: "A ticket for the Olivia Rodrigo show" describes three different products on The Unraveled Tour, sold on different terms. Most buying advice treats a ticket as one thing with a price attached. Here the terms attached to each type are the part that decides whether a listing you find later is a good deal or a partial one, and they are published — you do not have to guess.

sections.title: Find your date before comparing tickets
sections.content: [Choose your city and show on the Olivia Rodrigo date board](/artists/olivia-rodrigo). Match the venue and date, then open the checked ticket links shown for that event. Before comparing totals, establish whether each listing is a standard ticket, a VIP package or a ticket from a separate allocation programme. A resale listing's VIP label does not establish that the original package extras are included. Coverage varies by date, and a checked link does not guarantee current availability.

sections.title: Standard tickets: the delivery clock matters
sections.content:
The ordinary ticket is the one everything else is measured against, and two of its rules are worth knowing before you buy from anyone.

Ticketmaster's official help page for the tour states that the event organiser makes the scannable ticket available closer to the day of the event, estimated at around 48 hours beforehand, and that ticket transfer is available no later than three months before the event date. Read those together and a pattern falls out: for a long stretch before the show, a ticket exists as an entitlement rather than as a scannable thing, and transfer is due to become available by the three-month point. That is an opening deadline, not a statement that transfers close three months before the show. Once transfer is enabled, Ticketmaster says it can be used from the order before the event.

If you are buying from a resale marketplace, that is the mechanism behind a lot of ordinary-looking anxiety — a delayed barcode can be consistent with the organiser’s delivery schedule. It does not, by itself, verify that a resale purchase is valid or that a seller will deliver it. It is also why "when does it arrive" belongs in your decision rather than after it. The [guide to delivery and transfer timing](/guides/ticket-delivery-and-transfer-timing) goes through what to do when the two clocks do not line up.

sections.title: VIP packages: the extras do not travel
sections.content:
Live Nation's tour announcement points VIP buyers to VIP Nation, and Ticketmaster's help page sets out what a package contains. Its GA Early Entry Experience is described as one general admission ticket with priority access to the floor, a VIP laminate and lanyard, a specially designed VIP gift item, a photo opportunity in front of the VIP backdrop, pre-show tour merchandise shopping, early entry into the venue, and designated check-in with on-site VIP staff.

The backdrop photo opportunity does not include artist participation, according to Ticketmaster's package description. The part that matters second-hand is stated on the same page: merchandise, VIP package elements, fan club memberships and ticket insurance originally purchased with or included in a ticket are **not** transferable.

So a resale listing that says "VIP" may be transferring the seat and none of the things that made the package a package. That is not necessarily a bad buy — a floor ticket is a floor ticket — but it is a different purchase from the one the word implies, and it should be priced in your head accordingly. Before paying a premium for the label, ask the marketplace what is actually being transferred.

sections.title: Silver Star: check the request status
sections.content:
Silver Star uses a request-and-allocation process rather than an immediate purchase, and its windows are short. Ticketmaster’s help page gave the request window as closing on 2 September 2026, with successful requests confirmed by 9 September. Both of those dates have passed, so treat the process below as an explanation of how Silver Star works rather than a route that is open today, and check the official tour help page for any later release.

Tickets were offered in pairs, with a limit of two per person. Submitting a request did not guarantee an allocation. Ticketmaster says the card is charged only when a request can be fulfilled, and unsuccessful applicants can check their request status even if they receive no further email.

Use the official tour help page for the current country-specific instructions and any future release. Security checks during a request do not establish a resale or transfer policy, so do not infer that a second-hand Silver Star listing is permitted or prohibited from those checks alone. Confirm the terms attached to the actual ticket before paying.

No Silver Star price is repeated here: it is a separate official programme, not one of the ticket-site prices on the date list.

sections.title: What the artist page shows, and what it does not
sections.content:
On the [Olivia Rodrigo page](/artists/olivia-rodrigo), each verified date carries the ticket sites that have a checked destination for that exact show. Where a figure appears, it is one provider's listed price for that date at the time shown next to it — a resale marketplace's listing, not the tour's own pricing, and not a Silver Star or VIP figure. None of the three product types above is sold, allocated or issued by this site.

Which is the point of writing this down. The comparison worth making on this tour is not only between two figures, but between two things that are only superficially the same ticket. The [guide to official tickets versus resale](/guides/primary-vs-resale-concert-tickets) covers the general version; the specifics for this tour are on the official help page, and they are unusually clearly written.

posts.title: Why a price on this site disappears
posts.description: Saw a price on a ticket button earlier and now it's gone? Here's why that happens, and why the button still works.
posts.summary: A price that was on a ticket button an hour ago can be gone now. That's on purpose. A price only shows while it's fresh and checked, and a blank is better than an old number that looks current.
posts.author: TourTicketCompare

sections.content: You looked at a show this morning and a ticket button had a price on it. You've come back to buy and the price has gone: same show, same button, no number. Nothing is broken. The price got too old, or it stopped passing one of the checks behind it, and a blank is better than an old number that looks current.

sections.title: Prices only last a day
sections.content:
A price here is what one ticket site was asking for one show, at the time it was checked. Prices are re-checked through the day, and each card says how long ago its price was checked ("Checked 5 hours ago"). If a ticket site stops sending a price for that show, the last one stays up for a while with its age showing. Once it's more than 24 hours old, it comes down.

Nothing is quietly updated or left without a time. The price was right when it was checked, the card tells you when that was, and once it's too old to trust, it goes. [What a price on this site actually is](/blog/what-a-price-snapshot-actually-is) explains more.

sections.title: Every price has to pass a few checks
sections.content:
Age isn't the only thing. A price only shows if the ticket site allows it to be shown, it's for that exact show (not a nearby date), the link to that show has been checked, and the number itself looks like a real price. If any one of those fails, the price is hidden. There's no half-answer.

So a price can disappear because something changed about the show's link, not the price. If a link gets flagged for another look, or it turns out to point at the wrong show, any price attached to it comes down too.

sections.title: Some ticket sites never show a price
sections.content:
If a ticket site's button never has a price on it, that's down to the site, not the show. SeatGeek doesn't share its prices with this site, so its button is a checked link and nothing more. Ticket Liquidator doesn't share a price either, so it's link-only too. Ticketmaster is a plain link here.

A button with no price says nothing about how popular the show is.

sections.title: What doesn't happen when a price comes down
sections.content: No old price is kept up. No "from" price is made up. Nothing is averaged across sites, copied from another date or borrowed from another seat. And no site moves up the list because it still has a price: the order is always the same (sites that pay a commission first, Ticketmaster last), and it isn't a ranking. A blank beats an old number, and it beats a made-up one by a mile.

sections.title: What you're left with
sections.content:
The link. When a price comes down, the button stays, still checked, still going to that exact show. The ticket site is the only place to see the real, up-to-date total once fees, delivery and tax are added, so a missing price only costs you a starting point.

When a card does have a price, it also has a price history: up to 90 days of what that site was asking for that show. That's a better way to tell if today's price is unusual than any single number.

posts.title: How a ticket link gets published on TourTicketCompare
posts.seoTitle: How a ticket link gets published | TourTicketCompare
posts.description: What has to be true before a ticket button appears here, which checks a person does and which are automatic, and what happens when a link stops working.
posts.summary: Some of the checking behind a ticket button here is done by a person, and some is done automatically under strict rules. Here's which is which, and what happens when a link breaks.
posts.author: TourTicketCompare

sections.content: A ticket button only appears here once its link has been checked. If a link can't be checked, the page shows no button rather than a guess. Plenty of sites work the other way round, so here's what actually sits behind a button. "Verified" is a word worth pinning down before you trust it.

sections.title: A new artist starts with no buttons
sections.content:
When an artist is first added, their page is bare on purpose: a name, a short summary, and nothing else. No ticket buttons, no ticket-site logos, no dates. The page is also kept out of search results until it's ready.

There are two ways an artist gets their buttons. Either a person opens the link in a browser and checks three things: it loads, it's the right artist (not someone with the same name), and it's the ticket site's own page rather than a chain of redirects. Or it happens automatically, but only when both SeatGeek and Ticketmaster return an exact match for the name, Ticketmaster lists the act as music and not a tribute act, the name isn't on a block list, and both artist pages exist. No more than five artists a day go through that way, and any of them can be undone in one step.

sections.title: Show dates are added automatically
sections.content:
Checking an artist and checking a show date are different jobs. Dates, and most links to individual shows, are added automatically: new shows from Ticketmaster's official listings, a nightly pass that fixes details on shows already listed, and a separate check for each resale site.

What keeps that safe isn't a person at the end. It's that each check only adds a show when it's an exact match, runs the site's full set of tests on exactly what it's about to publish, and only goes ahead if they all pass. If a match isn't certain, it's flagged instead of added. If a ticket site doesn't answer properly, the existing details are left alone rather than wiped. For SeatGeek, for example, the show's time, city, venue and link all have to match SeatGeek's own listing.

That split is on purpose. Deciding a page belongs to the right artist is a judgement call, so either a person makes it or two separate sources have to agree exactly. Deciding a listing is the same show as one already on the site is a clear rule, so it's applied automatically, the same way every night, across far more dates than anyone could re-read by hand.

sections.title: Every link is checked again when you click
sections.content:
A saved link isn't trusted forever. Every time a button is shown, and again when you click it, the link is checked to make sure it still goes to the right site and the right show. If anything fails, the button doesn't appear. There's no fallback to a search page and no swapped-in link. No button is the honest answer.

It also means one ticket site's broken link doesn't take the others down. Each site's link stands on its own, so a date might have a checked link from one site, a plain link from another, and nothing from a third.

sections.title: Links break, and the site notices
sections.content:
A checked link was right when it was checked, so it gets checked again. A daily check runs through every saved link and reports any that stop working. It's careful about it: if a ticket site blocks the check (which some do to stop bots), that's noted as blocked, not broken, because it doesn't prove anything about the page. Real failures go to a person to fix.

A link is only removed when the ticket site clearly confirms the show is gone or doesn't match. Never because of one failed check, a login error or an empty reply that could just be a bad night.

sections.title: What a checked link doesn't promise
sections.content: Checked means the link is real and goes to that exact show. It doesn't mean the price is good, the seats are there, or the terms suit you. The ticket site sets all of that, and it changes all the time. If a link here is broken or goes to the wrong place, the [contact page](/contact) is the quickest way to flag it, and the [editorial policy](/editorial-policy) explains what gets fixed and how.

posts.title: What a price on this site actually means
posts.seoTitle: What a price on this site means | TourTicketCompare
posts.description: A price on a ticket button here is one ticket site's listed price for one show, with the time it was checked. Here's what that does and doesn't tell you.
posts.summary: When a ticket button here shows a price, it's one ticket site's listed price for that exact show, at the time shown. It's a handy starting point, not the price you'll pay at checkout.
posts.author: TourTicketCompare

sections.content: When a ticket button here shows a price, it's the lowest listed price one ticket site had for that show, at the time it was checked. That's a smaller promise than "price" usually means. On ticket sites, "price" can mean a starting figure, a price before fees, the price of the last two seats in a section, or what you actually pay.

sections.title: One site, one show, one moment
sections.content:
Each price comes from one ticket site, for one show, at one time. It isn't an average, a market rate, or your final total. Some fees may already be included. Check the full price for the number of tickets you want, with taxes, delivery and any extras, on the ticket site before you pay.

A price only shows if the ticket site allows it, it's for that exact show (not a nearby date), the link to the show has been checked, and it's recent enough. If any of those fails, there's no price on the button. A missing price is the site being careful, not a glitch.

sections.title: Why prices don't stay up forever
sections.content:
Prices move. A number with no time on it soon becomes a promise nobody can keep. So prices are re-checked through the day, each one shows how long ago it was checked ("Checked 5 hours ago"), and once one is more than 24 hours old it comes down.

That's why every price here has its age next to it. The time isn't small print. It's what makes the number trustworthy.

sections.title: Not every ticket site has a price
sections.content:
Ticket sites share different things. Vivid Seats, TicketNetwork and StubHub International share their listed prices and allow them to be shown, so their buttons can carry one. SeatGeek doesn't share prices with this site, so its button is always a plain checked link. Ticket Liquidator doesn't share a price either. Ticketmaster is a plain link here.

So one show might have prices from two sites and plain links to three more. That's an honest picture, not a messy one.

sections.title: What the button order means
sections.content:
Buttons always appear in the same order: sites that pay this site a commission first, Ticketmaster (which pays nothing) last. The page says so next to the buttons. It isn't a ranking, and nothing sorts by price or points at a "best" option.

That's because prices checked at different times aren't a fair head-to-head. One price is only called lower than another when both are fresh and for the same show. And nothing here claims tickets are still available: the site can't see how many are left, and it won't pretend to.

What a price here is good for is a quick shortlist before you open two or three tabs. Your real total is on the ticket site's order screen, after fees, delivery and tax. [The guide to ticket fees](/guides/concert-ticket-fees-explained) explains what usually gets added along the way.

posts.title: Why some artist pages here show no dates
posts.seoTitle: Why some artist pages show no dates | TourTicketCompare
posts.description: An artist page with no upcoming shows usually means the tour has finished. Here's what an empty page means and what it offers instead.
posts.summary: At any time, plenty of artist pages here have no upcoming dates. That's usually just a finished tour, and the page changes what it offers when it happens.
posts.author: TourTicketCompare

sections.content: If you land on an artist page here and there are no tour dates, the most likely reason is the boring one: the tour has finished and the last date has passed. The page doesn't hide that or pad itself out. It says so, and then it gives you something else to do.

sections.title: An empty page isn't a broken page
sections.content:
Each artist page is built from that artist's show dates. When the last upcoming date passes, it isn't deleted. It just stops being upcoming, and the list empties. Nothing is removed and nothing is made up to fill the gap.

What changes is what the page says. The heading stops promising tour dates, the summary shown in search changes to match, and the dates are replaced by a plain note: there are no confirmed upcoming dates yet, and no way to know yet whether more are coming. The dates that just passed stay underneath for reference, clearly marked as over.

The page itself stays up and stays in search, so it's there the moment new dates are announced. (The one exception is an artist who has never had a date on the site: their page stays out of search until their first date arrives.) One honest page at the same address beats a page that keeps vanishing and coming back.

sections.title: The ticket buttons go too
sections.content:
With no dates, there are no date cards, so there are no buttons for individual shows. At most, the page offers one clearly labelled link to the artist's page on a ticket site ("See the artist on SeatGeek", for example), if that link has been checked. It goes to the artist, not a show, and it doesn't pretend to be a date. The show buttons come back with the dates.

Next to it you'll find the recent dates and a form to leave your email, so you hear as soon as confirmed dates go up for that artist.

sections.title: Artist lists don't oversell it either
sections.content:
An honest page isn't much use if every link to it suggests otherwise. So the artist lists across the site follow the same rule. An artist with no upcoming dates is marked "No dates currently listed", offers a date alert instead of a ticket link, and sits in a second group below the artists who do have shows.

You can still click through, because the page is still useful. It just doesn't take up a spot meant for artists with shows. You should never click from a list of tour dates to a page that has none.

sections.title: What an empty page doesn't mean
sections.content:
It doesn't mean the artist has no tour. It means this site doesn't have a date for them yet. The site covers artists one by one, dates come in from Ticketmaster's listings through a daily check, and each ticket button only goes up once its link has been checked. If you know a date is missing, the [contact page](/contact) is the quickest way to flag it.

It isn't a comment on the artist either. Empty pages mostly show up between one tour ending and the next being announced, which is where most acts spend a good chunk of any year.

sections.title: If you're waiting for tickets to go on sale
sections.content: That gap is also when ticket scams spike, because people want tickets and there's nothing real to buy yet. Two things worth reading while you wait: [how to prepare for an on-sale](/guides/how-to-prepare-for-a-ticket-onsale), and [how to spot fake listings](/guides/how-to-avoid-ticket-scams) before the real dates arrive.
